claim: All primate cortical shapes can be described as a set of nested folds of different sizes.
source: We show that all cortical shapes can be described as a set of nested folds of different sizes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: As neighbouring folds are gradually merged, the cortices of 11 primate species follow a common scale-free morphometric trajectory.
source: As neighbouring folds are gradually merged, the cortices of 11 primate species follow a common scale-free morphometric trajectory, that also overlaps with over 70 other mammalian species.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data presented in Figure 2.

claim: The morphometric trajectory of 11 primate species overlaps with over 70 other mammalian species.
source: As neighbouring folds are gradually merged, the cortices of 11 primate species follow a common scale-free morphometric trajectory, that also overlaps with over 70 other mammalian species.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by comparative data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 3D.

claim: All cerebral cortices are approximations of the same archetypal fractal shape with a fractal dimension of df = 2.5.
source: Our results indicate that all cerebral cortices are approximations of the same archetypal fractal shape with a fractal dimension of df = 2.5.
evidence: This is a main conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by scaling analysis in the results.

claim: There is a scale-dependent effect of ageing on brain morphology.
source: To demonstrate the importance of this new understanding, we show a scale-dependent effect of ageing on brain morphology.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated with data in Figure 4.

claim: There is a more than fourfold increase in effect size (from two standard deviations to eight standard deviations) at a spatial scale of approximately 2 mm compared to standard morphological analyses.
source: We observe a more than fourfold increase in effect size (from two standard deviations to eight standard deviations) at a spatial scale of approximately 2 mm compared to standard morphological analyses.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The mammalian cerebral cortex exhibits a large diversity of shapes and sizes across and within species.
source: The morphological complexity of the mammalian cerebral cortex has fascinated scientists for generations, with cortices across and within species, exhibiting a large diversity of shapes and sizes.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The mammalian brain folds into stereotypical, hierarchically-organised structures such as lobes and major gyri.
source: The mammalian brain folds into stereotypical, hierarchically-organised structures such as lobes and major gyri.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Qualitative and quantitative regularities in cortical scaling have often been suggested and observed.
source: In fact, qualitative and quantitative regularities in cortical scaling have often been suggested and observed (Zhang and Sejnowski, 2000; Francis et al., 2009; Karbowski, 2011; Mota and Herculano-Houzel, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The scaling law AtT^(1/2)=kAe^(5/4) was shown to be valid across mammalian species.
source: This scaling law, relating powers of cortical thickness and surface area metrics, was shown to be valid across mammalian species (Mota and Herculano-Houzel, 2015) and within the human species (Wang et al., 2016), as well as to the structures and substructures of individual brains (Wang et al., 2019; Leiberg et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The scaling law AtT^(1/2)=kAe^(5/4) was shown to be valid within the human species.
source: This scaling law, relating powers of cortical thickness and surface area metrics, was shown to be valid across mammalian species (Mota and Herculano-Houzel, 2015) and within the human species (Wang et al., 2016), as well as to the structures and substructures of individual brains (Wang et al., 2019; Leiberg et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The scaling law AtT^(1/2)=kAe^(5/4) was shown to be valid for structures and substructures of individual brains.
source: This scaling law, relating powers of cortical thickness and surface area metrics, was shown to be valid across mammalian species (Mota and Herculano-Houzel, 2015) and within the human species (Wang et al., 2016), as well as to the structures and substructures of individual brains (Wang et al., 2019; Leiberg et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The universality of the scaling law is presumed to arise from universal physical principles and evolutionarily conserved biomechanics.
source: However, this universality, presumed to be arising from universal physical principles and evolutionarily conserved biomechanics, says little about what that cortical shape actually is, beyond a constraint binding three morphometric parameters.
evidence: This is stated as a presumption or speculation about the underlying mechanisms.

claim: Coarse-grained primate cortices at each spatial scale can be understood as approximations of the same universal self-similar archetypal form.
source: Specifically, we introduce a coarse-graining procedure that renders the cortex at different spatial scales, or resolutions. We show that coarse-grained primate cortices at each spatial scale can be understood as approximations of the same universal self-similar archetypal form, of which the observed scaling law Equation 1 can then be shown to be a direct consequence.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study stated in the introduction.

claim: The observed scaling law Equation 1 is a direct consequence of cortices being approximations of the same universal self-similar archetypal form.
source: We show that coarse-grained primate cortices at each spatial scale can be understood as approximations of the same universal self-similar archetypal form, of which the observed scaling law Equation 1 can then be shown to be a direct consequence.
evidence: This is stated as a finding that connects the scaling law to the universal form.

claim: The results indicate a conservation of morphological relationships across evolution.
source: Besides revealing a symmetry in nature hidden under much apparent complexity, our results indicate a conservation of morphological relationships across evolution.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the results.

claim: The effects of human ageing on cortical morphology are highly scale-dependent.
source: As an example, we will calculate the effects of human ageing across spatial scales and show that the effects are highly scale-dependent.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and demonstrated with data in Figure 4.

claim: In fractal scaling, the scaling or power exponent between the measured intrinsic and extrinsic sizes is the fractal dimension.
source: The scaling, or power exponent between the measured intrinsic and extrinsic sizes is the so-called fractal dimension.
evidence: This is stated as a definition from fractal geometry.

claim: Many structures in nature, particularly in biology, are good approximations of a fractal.
source: Although actual fractals are mathematical abstractions, they can often be defined as the limit of iterative processes. Many structures in nature, and in particular biology (Elston and Zietsch, 2005; Codling et al., 2008; Ionescu et al., 2009; Losa, 2011; Klonowski, 2016; Di Ieva, 2016; Reznikov et al., 2018), are good approximations of a fractal.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with multiple citations.

claim: Fractal scaling for various aspects of cortical morphology has often been postulated.
source: Indeed, fractal scaling for various aspects of cortical morphology has often been postulated (Free et al., 1996; Kiselev et al., 2003), with a number of recent papers making use of MRI data (Marzi et al., 2021; Jao et al., 2021; Meregalli et al., 2022; Díaz Beltrán et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Most recently published estimates of fractal dimension for the whole cortex are close to 2.5.
source: Most recently published estimates of fractal dimension for the whole cortex are indeed close to 2.5 (King et al., 2010; Madan and Kensinger, 2016; Madan and Kensinger, 2017; Marzi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: The coarse-graining method removes morphological details smaller than a specified scale while preserving surface integrity.
source: This is achieved through a coarse-graining method that removes morphological details smaller than a specified scale while preserving surface integrity.
evidence: This is a description of the method developed in the study.

claim: At a set scale of 3 mm, sulcal walls that are less than 3 mm apart would be removed, and the neighbouring gyri would be fused.
source: For example, at a set scale of 3 mm, sulcal walls that are less than 3 mm apart would be removed, and the neighbouring gyri would be fused.
evidence: This is an example illustrating how the coarse-graining method works.

claim: The coarse-graining method is a new systematic way of obtaining shape properties from the cortex in terms of a sequence of morphometric measurements as spatial scale varies.
source: This method is a new systematic way of obtaining shape properties from the cortex in terms of a sequence of morphometric measurements as spatial scale varies.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the methodological contribution.

claim: The box-counting algorithm fills an object with boxes or voxels of increasingly larger sizes and counts the number of boxes in the object as a function of box size.
source: Briefly, this algorithm fills the object of interest (the cortex in our case) with boxes, or voxels of increasingly larger sizes and counts the number of boxes in the object as a function of box size.
evidence: This is a description of the established box-counting algorithm.

claim: In a log-log plot of box-counting results, the slope of the relationship between number of boxes and box size indicates the fractal dimension of the object.
source: As the box size increases, the number of boxes decreases; and in a log-log plot, the slope of this relationship indicates the fractal dimension of the object.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the box-counting method.

claim: With increasing box size in the box-counting method, the smaller details below the resolution of a single box would disappear first, and increasingly larger details will follow.
source: Intuitively, with increasing box size, the smaller details below the resolution of a single box would disappear first, and increasingly larger details will follow – precisely what we require from a coarse-graining method.
evidence: This is stated as an intuitive explanation of how the method works.

claim: The coarse-graining method requires the bounding pial and white matter surfaces of the cortical ribbon as input.
source: Concretely, our proposed method requires the bounding pial and white matter surfaces of the cortical ribbon as input.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological requirement.

claim: At any given scale, the voxelisation process effectively erases morphological features (folds) that are smaller than the cube size.
source: At any given scale, or voxel size, this process effectively erases morphological features (folds) that are smaller than the cube size.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the method.

claim: Increasing the voxel size visually appears as if the cortex is 'melting' and 'thickening'.
source: Visually, increasing the voxel size appear as if the cortex is 'melting' and 'thickening' (Figure 1, and videos: https://bit.ly/3CDoqZQ).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The coarse-graining method has no direct dependency on the original MR image resolution.
source: Note this method has also no direct dependency on the original MR image resolution, as the inputs are smooth grey and white matter surface meshes reconstructed from the images using strong (bio-)physical assumptions and, therefore, containing more fine-grained spatial information than the raw images (see also Appendix 2).
evidence: This is stated as a property of the method.

claim: An isometric rescaling process is applied to analyse the scaling behaviour of different coarse-grained realisations of the same brain.
source: Therefore, to analyse the scaling behaviour of the different coarse-grained realisations of the same brain, we apply an isometric rescaling process that leaves all dimensionless shape properties unaffected (more details in Appendix 3.1).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological step.

claim: The rescaling process fixes the voxel size and resizes the surfaces relative to the voxel size.
source: Conceptually, this process fixes the voxel size, and instead resizes the surfaces relative to the voxel size, which ensures that we can compare the coarse-grained realisations to the original cortices, and test if the former, like the latter, also scales according to Equation 1.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation of the rescaling procedure.

claim: After rescaling, cortical thickness shrinks with increasing levels of coarse-graining and never exceeds the thickness measured at native scale.
source: After rescaling, as an example, the cortical thickness also shrinks with increasing levels of coarse-graining, and never exceeds the thickness measured at native scale.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the rescaled data.

claim: All cortical surface reconstructions except marmoset data were based on healthy individual brains.
source: With the exception of the marmoset data, all other cortical surface reconstructions were based on healthy individual brains.
evidence: This is stated in the data and processing section.

claim: Human Connectome Project MRI data was obtained using a 3T Siemens Skyra scanner with 0.7 mm isotropic voxel size.
source: To study healthy human adults, we used the Human Connectome Project (HCP) MRI data, available at https://db.humanconnectome.org/; Van Essen et al., 2012, obtained using a 3T Siemens Skyra scanner with 0.7 mm isotropic voxel size.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the data acquisition.

claim: Cam-CAN used a 3T Siemens TIM Trio System with 1 mm isotropic voxel size.
source: Cam-CAN used a 3T Siemens TIM Trio System with 1 mm isotropic voxel size (for more details see Shafto et al., 2014; Taylor et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the data acquisition with citations.

claim: From the Cam-CAN dataset, 644 subjects successfully completed preprocessing without errors.
source: From the Cam-CAN dataset we retained 644 subjects that successfully completed preprocessing (with Freesurfer recon-all) without errors.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the data processing.

claim: The 20 y.o. cohort from Cam-CAN consisted of 27 subjects between the ages of 17–25 inclusive.
source: From these subjects, we selected all subjects between the ages of 17–25 inclusive (forming the 20 y.o. cohort, n=27)
evidence: This is stated as a description of the cohort selection.

claim: The 80 y.o. cohort from Cam-CAN consisted of 86 subjects between the ages of 77–85 inclusive.
source: we also selected all subjects between the ages of 77–85 inclusive (forming the 80 y.o. cohort, n=86).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the cohort selection.

claim: Rhesus Macaque MRI scans were carried out at the Newcastle University Comparative Biology Centre with macaques trained to be scanned while awake.
source: Rhesus Macaque MRI scans were carried out at the Newcastle University Comparative Biology Centre. Macaques were trained to be scanned while awake and sat in a primate chair.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the data acquisition.

claim: The marmoset MRI structural scan was collected ex vivo from a 4.5-year-old male marmoset.
source: Data was collected ex vivo from a 4.5-year-old male marmoset using a T2-star weighted 3D FLASH sequence using a horizontal MRI scanner (Biospec 7 Tesla, Bruker Biospin, Ettlingen, Germany).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the data acquisition.

claim: Different primate species overlap substantially in offset and only differ in the range of scales over which the approximation is valid.
source: Considering all species together, different species also overlap substantially (similar offset), and only differ from each other in the range of scales over which the approximation is valid (see Appendix 3.2 and Appendix 4).
evidence: This is stated as a result with reference to appendices.

claim: Coarse-grained primate cortices are morphometrically similar to actual existing mammalian cortices.
source: Thus, coarse-grained primate cortices are morphometrically similar to, and in terms of the universal law, 'as valid as' actual existing mammalian cortices.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the analysis.

claim: The coarse-grained brain surfaces are not to be directly likened to actual brain surfaces in terms of the location or shape of the folds.
source: Note, of course, that the coarse-grained brain surfaces are an output of our algorithm alone and not to be directly/naively likened to actual brain surfaces, e.g., in terms of the location or shape of the folds.
evidence: This is stated as a clarification about the interpretation of results.

claim: The comparisons between coarse-grained brains and actual brains is purely on the level of morphometrics across the whole cortex.
source: Our comparisons here between coarse-grained brains and actual brains is purely on the level of morphometrics across the whole cortex.
evidence: This is stated as a clarification about the scope of comparisons.

claim: Non-brain objects like walnut and bell pepper vary in both K and S, unlike primate brains.
source: In contrast, we tested various non-brain objects, and while e.g., the walnut, and bell pepper form (partially) straight lines, they vary in both K and S (see Appendix 5).
evidence: This is stated as a result with reference to Appendix 5.

claim: For scales over ∼5 mm and under ∼0.5 mm, the differences in At between age groups become relatively small.
source: For scales over ∼5 mm, and under ∼0.5 mm the differences become relatively small, suggesting the ageing process has less effect on the largest and smallest cortical morphological features.
evidence: This is stated as a result with an interpretation.

claim: The ageing results were reproduced in an independent dataset.
source: Finally, we reproduced these results in an independent dataset in Appendix 7.2.
evidence: This is stated as a validation of the results.

claim: On a scale of 0.27 mm, the gyri in younger subjects are densely packed, but older subjects show widening between gyral walls and decrease in gyral surface area at the crown.
source: On a scale of 0.27 mm, the gyri in the younger subjects are densely packed, but the older subjects show the expected widening between gyral walls and decrease in gyral surface area at the crown (see e.g. Jin et al., 2018; Madan, 2019; Kochunov et al., 2008 for recent investigations and references therein).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with citations to supporting literature.

claim: At 1.86 mm scale, younger cortices have partially 'melted,' erasing most small sulci between densely packed gyri.
source: At 1.86 mm, the younger cortices have already partially 'melted,' erasing most small sulci between the densely packed gyri.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the analysis.

claim: At 1.86 mm scale, in older humans the gyri are less dense, the sulci is more open, and most gyri and sulci have not been erased yet.
source: In the older humans, however, the gyri are less dense, the sulci is more open, and thus, at 1.86 mm, most gyri and sulci have not been erased yet.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the analysis.

claim: At scale 7.94 mm, both young and old brains have 'melted' down to similarly near-lissencephalic cortices.
source: At scale 7.94 mm, both young and old brains have 'melted' down to similarly near-lissencephalic cortices.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the analysis.

claim: The melting process can be regarded as a way of determining how cortical area is allocated across different scales.
source: More broadly, one can regard the melting process as a way of determining how cortical area is allocated across different scales.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the method.

claim: The study devised a new way of expressing the morphology of the mammalian cerebral cortex as the flow in the values of morphometric measures over a range of spatial scales.
source: We have devised a new way of expressing the morphology of the mammalian cerebral cortex, as the flow in the values of morphometric measures over a range of spatial scales.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the methodological contribution.

claim: All diverse primate cortices are approximations of the same archetypal self-similar (fractal) shape.
source: After applying this method to the cortices of 11 primate species, we have shown that all these diverse cortices are approximations of the same archetypal self-similar (fractal) shape.
evidence: This is stated as a main conclusion of the study.

claim: Most of the morphological diversity of primate cortices can be ascribed to the species-specific ranges of spatial scales over which each approximation is valid.
source: Most of their morphological diversity can be ascribed to the species-specific ranges of spatial scales over which each approximation is valid, with the smallest scale being an invariant multiple of cortical thickness.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the results.

claim: The smallest scale in the fractal approximation is an invariant multiple of cortical thickness.
source: Most of their morphological diversity can be ascribed to the species-specific ranges of spatial scales over which each approximation is valid, with the smallest scale being an invariant multiple of cortical thickness.
evidence: This is stated as a finding about the scaling behavior.

claim: The coarse-graining method is a proof-by-construction of fractality, a step beyond the usual box-counting approach.
source: This was a proof-by-construction of fractality, a step beyond the usual box-counting approach, which also yields scale-dependent morphometrics.
evidence: This is stated as a characterization of the methodological advance.

claim: Healthy human ageing has highly scale-dependent effects in a range of morphometrics.
source: As a proof-of-principle we showed that healthy human ageing has highly scale-dependent effects in a range of morphometrics.
evidence: This is stated as a proof-of-principle result.

claim: This is the first time showing that representative primate species follow the exact same fractal scaling.
source: Compared to previous literature, we can summarise our main contribution and advance as follows: (i) We are showing for the first time that representative primate species follow the exact same fractal scaling – as opposed to previous work showing that they have a similar fractal dimension (Hofman, 1985; Hofman, 1991), i.e., slope, but not necessarily the same offset, as previous methods had no consistent way of comparing offsets.
evidence: This is stated as a novel contribution with citations to previous work.

claim: Previous work showed that primate species have a similar fractal dimension but not necessarily the same offset.
source: as opposed to previous work showing that they have a similar fractal dimension (Hofman, 1985; Hofman, 1991), i.e., slope, but not necessarily the same offset, as previous methods had no consistent way of comparing offsets.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of previous work with citations.

claim: Previous work could not show direct agreement in morphometrics between coarse-grained brains of primate species and other non-primate mammalian species.
source: (ii) Previous work could also not show direct agreement in morphometrics between the coarse-grained brains of primate species and other non-primate mammalian species.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of previous work.

claim: Multiscale morphometrics can have much larger effect sizes for classification applications compared to single-scale metrics.
source: (iii) Demonstrating in proof-of-principle that multiscale morphometrics, in practice, can have much larger effect sizes for classification applications.
evidence: This is stated as a practical contribution of the study.

claim: Representative primate brains and mammalian brains share a range of key shape properties on top of agreeing in fractal dimension.
source: However, we demonstrate here, that representative primate brains and mammalian brains indeed share a range of other key shape properties, on top of agreeing in fractal dimension.
evidence: This is stated as a main finding of the study.

claim: The results suggest a universal blueprint for mammalian brain shape and a common set of mechanisms governing cortical folding.
source: This suggests a universal blueprint for mammalian brain shape and a common set of mechanisms governing cortical folding.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the results.

claim: The novel method of deriving multiscale metrics can differentiate subtle morphological changes four times better than metrics at a single native scale.
source: As a practical additional outcome of our study, we could show that our novel method of deriving multiscale metrics can differentiate subtle morphological changes much better (four times the effect size) than the metrics we have been using so far at a single native scale.
evidence: This is stated as a practical outcome of the study.

claim: Expressing cortical morphology as a function of scale is more detailed than a list of summary morphometric measures.
source: Expressing cortical morphology as a function of scale is more detailed than a list of summary morphometric measures, and more informative than the mere listing of every sulcus and gyrus.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the new approach.

claim: Some biological processes may only act on specific spatial scales, leaving other scales untouched.
source: A clear advantage is that some biological processes may only act on a specific spatial scales, leaving other scales untouched (ageing in our example).
evidence: This is stated as an advantage with ageing as an example.

claim: The approach allows for disambiguation of spatial scale, providing an extra dimension of understanding and tracking of biological processes.
source: By disambiguation of the spatial scale, it allows for an extra dimension of understanding, and tracking of biological processes.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the method.

claim: The approach can be extended to cortical development and various degenerative and congenital neuropathic conditions.
source: In the future, this approach can also be extended to cortical development and to various degenerative (Wang et al., 2016) and congenital (Wang et al., 2021) neuropathic conditions, especially if combined with a regionalised versions of this method applied to specific cortical regions (Wang et al., 2019) or local patches (Leiberg et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as a future direction with citations to relevant work.

claim: The main result is the demonstration of a universal self-similar scaling for primate, and presumably mammalian cortices.
source: Empirically, the main result of this paper is the demonstration of a universal self-similar scaling (Equation 3) for primate, and presumably mammalian cortices.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the main empirical result.

claim: The dual universality in K suggests the existence of a single highly conserved mechanism for cortical folding operating on all length scales self-similarly.
source: However, the fact that both universalities hold true is significant. It suggests the existence of a single highly conserved mechanism for cortical folding, operating on all length scales self-similarly with only a few morphological degrees of freedom.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the dual universality.

claim: The dual universality hints at the possibility of deriving cortical scaling from some variational principle.
source: It also hints at the possibility of deriving cortical scaling from some variational principle.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about theoretical implications.

claim: The dual universality is a more stringent test for existing and future models of cortical gyrification mechanisms.
source: Finally, this dual universality is also a more stringent test for existing and future models of cortical gyrification mechanisms at relevant scales, and one that moreover is applicable to individual cortices.
evidence: This is stated as an implication for model validation.

claim: Models that simulate a cortical surface could be directly coarse-grained with the method and morphological trajectories compared with actual cortices.
source: For example, any models that explicitly simulate a cortical surface as an output could be directly coarse-grained with our method and the morphological trajectories can be compared with those of actual humans and primate cortices.
evidence: This is stated as a potential application for model validation.

claim: Simulated cortices would only be 'valid' in terms of dual universality if they produce the same morphological trajectories.
source: The simulated cortices would only be 'valid' in terms of the dual universality, if it also produces the same morphological trajectories
evidence: This is stated as a criterion for model validity.

claim: The scaling itself does not imply or favour any particular proposed gyrification model.
source: The scaling itself does not imply or favour any particular proposed gyrification model (ours Mota and Herculano-Houzel, 2015 included), and all results in this paper are agnostic about this choice.
evidence: This is stated as a clarification about the interpretation of results.

claim: The previously proposed model for cortical gyrification assumes only a self-avoiding cortex of finite thickness experiencing pressures.
source: Indeed, our previously proposed model (Mota and Herculano-Houzel, 2015) for cortical gyrification is very simple, assuming only a self-avoiding cortex of finite thickness experiencing pressures (e.g. exerted by white matter pulling, or by CSF pressure).
evidence: This is stated as a description of a previous model with citation.

claim: There are challenges to the axonal tension hypothesis.
source: However, there are also challenges to the axonal tension hypothesis (Xu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to work challenging the hypothesis.

claim: White matter tension differentials in the developed brain may not explain the location of folds, but may contribute to whole-brain scale 'pressure' during development.
source: Indeed, white matter tension differentials in the developed brain may not explain the location of folds, but instead white matter tension may contribute to a whole-brain scale 'pressure' during development that drives the folding process overall.
evidence: This is stated as an alternative interpretation.

claim: The simplicity of the scaling law parallels many complex phenomena in nature that display simple and universal scaling derivable from first principles.
source: Aside from speculations about the biological interpretation, the simplicity of the highlighted scaling law parallels many complex phenomena in nature that displays simple and universal scaling that can be derived from first principles (Barenblatt, 1996; West et al., 1997; Gagler et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated as an analogy with citations to examples from physics.

claim: Recent results suggest simplicity and symmetry are generically favoured on statistical-ensemble grounds by evolution.
source: In addition, recent results suggest simplicity and symmetry are generically favoured on statistical-ensemble grounds by evolution (Johnston et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to recent work.

claim: The model correctly predicts the scaling law (Equation 1), but a more complete explanation for cortical gyrification is probably far more complex.
source: Our model correctly predicts the scaling law (Equation 1), but a more complete explanation for cortical gyrification is probably far more complex (Quezada et al., 2020) than can be accounted by such a simple model.
evidence: This is stated as an acknowledgment of model limitations with citation.

claim: The exact patterns, locations, depth, and features of gyri and sulci are variable but somewhat heritable in humans.
source: One specific example of said complexity is the exact patterns, locations, depth, and features of gyri and sulci. We know such patterns to be, for example, variable but also somewhat heritable in humans, whilst in macaques such patterns are relatively preserved across the species.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cortical patterns.

claim: In macaques, gyri and sulci patterns are relatively preserved across the species.
source: whilst in macaques such patterns are relatively preserved across the species.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about macaque cortical patterns.

claim: The work does not explain the variability or heritability of gyri and sulci patterns.
source: Our work does not explain any of these observations, nor are the coarse-grained versions of human brains is supposed to exactly resemble the location/pattern/features of gyri and sulci of other primates.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the current work.

claim: The similarities highlighted are on the level of summary metrics, pointing towards highly conserved quantities and mechanisms.
source: The similarities we highlighted here are on the level of summary metrics, and our goal was to highlight the universality in such metrics points towards highly conserved quantities and mechanisms.
evidence: This is stated as a clarification of the scope and interpretation of results.

claim: The scaling law can be understood as physically and biologically plausible statements.
source: The scaling law can, therefore, be understood as a physically and biologically plausible statements and our algorithm yields results in line with the scaling law.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the biological plausibility.

claim: The interaction between brain development and evolution may benefit from a scale-specific understanding.
source: More broadly, the interaction between brain development and evolution may also benefit from a scale-specific understanding.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about broader implications.

claim: The larger the cortical feature, the earlier during development it appears.
source: Generally, the larger the cortical feature (i.e. from gyri to functional areas to lobes to hemispheres), the earlier during development it appears (Zilles et al., 2013; Garcia et al., 2018), and more broadly it is conserved over kinship (Pizzagalli et al., 2020) and phylogeny (Heuer et al., 2019; Valk et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Larger cortical features are more broadly conserved over kinship and phylogeny.
source: Generally, the larger the cortical feature (i.e. from gyri to functional areas to lobes to hemispheres), the earlier during development it appears (Zilles et al., 2013; Garcia et al., 2018), and more broadly it is conserved over kinship (Pizzagalli et al., 2020) and phylogeny (Heuer et al., 2019; Valk et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Comparative neuroanatomical methods may be used to identify and contrast structures in coarse-grained cortices of more highly gyrified species with their analogues in less-gyrified species.
source: It thus seems likely that comparative neuroanatomical methods (Mars et al., 2014; Croxson et al., 2018) may be directly used to identify and contrast structures in coarse-grained cortices of more highly gyrified species with their analogues in less-gyrified species.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about potential applications with citations.

claim: The surface area difference between older and younger subjects at the 'native' scale is negligible (effect size smaller than two standard deviations).
